questions.explain: gp3 bundles a baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s with per-GB-month pricing, with extra IOPS up to 16,000 at ~$0.005/IOPS-month; io1/io2 make you declare an IOPS number and pay per provisioned IOPS-month (~$0.10–$0.125) whether used or not, plus storage. SQL Server I/O is spiky (checkpoints, tempdb spills, log writes can be 5–10x the average), so resolve peak-vs-average tension with measured P50/P95/P99.9 percentiles.
options: gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS with per-GB pricing and cheap extra IOPS ($0.005/IOPS-month); io1/io2 charges per provisioned IOPS-month regardless of use; SQL Server I/O bursts 5–10x average, so measure P50/P95/P99.9 before deciding
Both models charge identically per IOPS

questions.q: What are the two storage pricing models, and what is SQL Server's I/O wrinkle?

questions.explain: The chapter's three insights: gp3 extra-IOPS pricing (~$0.005/IOPS-month) is roughly 25x cheaper than io2 (~$0.125); between ~3,000 and 16,000 IOPS gp3 with extra provisioned IOPS almost always wins on cost; genuine io2 workloads (sustained 20,000+ IOPS or hard sub-ms latency SLAs) are rare — and every 1,000 IOPS tuned away saves ~$125/month permanently.
options: io2 is cheaper at every IOPS level
gp3 wins on cost for almost everything under 16,000 IOPS (extra IOPS ~25x cheaper than io2); io2 is justified only for sustained 20,000+ IOPS or hard sub-millisecond latency SLAs
The break-even is exactly 3,000 IOPS for all volumes
Storage type has no effect on cost

questions.explain: Attribute I/O with sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats: tempdb-dominated writes → query tuning (fix spills) rather than faster storage; log-dominated I/O → check log backup frequency and long-running transactions (FULL vs SIMPLE recovery); only the residual I/O after tuning should drive the gp3 vs io2 decision.
options: Attribution is impossible; just buy the fastest storage
Only CloudWatch matters, not SQL Server DMVs
Always buy io2 when tempdb is busy

questions.explain: Worked example: 1TB, sustained 12,000 IOPS → gp3 $160/month vs io2 $1,625/month (gp3 wins 10x). At 40,000 IOPS sustained, gp3 maxes at 16,000 and cannot serve the workload at all — io2 at $5,125/month is the only option, and the real question becomes whether tuning can bring it below 16,000 to unlock gp3.
options: At 12,000 IOPS sustained on 1TB: gp3 ≈ $160/mo vs io2 ≈ $1,625/mo — gp3 wins; at 40,000 IOPS sustained, gp3's 16,000 ceiling can't serve it, so io2 is the only option (or tune below 16,000)
io2 is always cheaper above 3,000 IOPS
gp3 can serve any IOPS level

questions.q: Walk through the chapter's two worked break-even examples.

questions.explain: Run a monthly job (Lambda/Azure Function) that pulls 30 days of ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS, computes P50/P95/P99.9, plugs them into the break-even formula, and posts a recommendation when the cheaper option saves more than ~$200/month — but keep the actual switch human-approved, since automation can't see latency SLAs or maintenance windows. After switching, validate against the bill (Cost Explorer line items within one billing cycle) and confirm P99 latency didn't regress.
options: Automate the storage-type switch to run unattended daily
Never re-analyze; one break-even calculation lasts forever
Monthly automated break-even recomputation with human-approved switches; post-switch validate the bill (Cost Explorer within one cycle) and P99 latency
Only validate metrics, never the bill
